title: SQL ANY and SOME Operators
learningObjectives: Explain the purpose and behaviour of SQL ANY and SOME Operators.
Write valid SQLite queries that demonstrate the topic or a documented equivalent.
Predict result rows using the supplied sample data.
Identify common mistakes and important NULL or duplicate behaviour.
Choose an appropriate query pattern for a practical reporting task.

understand.concept: ANY (also called SOME in SQL) is used with a comparison operator and a subquery. The comparison is true when it is true for at least one value returned by the subquery. If the subquery is empty, ANY is false. NULL values can produce UNKNOWN when no comparison is true.
understand.whyItMatters: ANY is useful when a value should be compared with a set of candidate values, such as finding products priced above at least one price in a selected category.
understand.analogy: Think of a database report as carefully combining or grouping rows from well-labelled registers to answer a specific question.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not model SQL's exact evaluation rules, duplicate semantics, three-valued NULL logic or dialect-specific features.

examples.title: Find products priced above at least one target (EXISTS rewrite)
examples.explanation: For this non-NULL target set, EXISTS expresses the ANY comparison: at least one target is lower than the product price.

examples.title: Find products cheaper than at least one target
examples.explanation: A product qualifies when its price is lower than one or more target prices.

examples.title: Compare with any target using a scalar minimum
examples.explanation: For a non-empty set with no NULL values, greater than ANY is equivalent to greater than the minimum value.

examples.title: Find products that match at least one exact target
examples.explanation: No product price equals any target price, so the existence test returns no products.

examples.title: Find products above at least one selected target
examples.explanation: The subquery can filter the comparison set before testing whether any comparison succeeds.

practise.guidedTask: Study the ANY syntax in the explanation. Run the equivalent correlated EXISTS queries in the SQLite Playground, then compare the result with a MIN-based rewrite on the supplied non-NULL data.
practise.independentTask: Create candidates and qualifying_scores tables. Write a portable SQLite EXISTS rewrite for candidates scoring above at least one qualifying score. Then document the equivalent ANY syntax for a DBMS that supports quantified comparisons.
hints: ANY requires a comparison operator followed by a subquery.
ANY is true when at least one comparison is true.
SOME is a synonym for ANY in supported SQL dialects.
SQLite does not implement quantified ANY/SOME syntax; use EXISTS for the executable exercises.
MIN rewrites require a non-empty comparison set and careful NULL handling.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of SQL ANY and SOME Operators?
options: ANY (also called SOME in SQL) is used with a comparison operator and a subquery
To permanently change the database schema
To disable query filtering
To create a new database connection
questions.answer: ANY (also called SOME in SQL) is used with a comparison operator and a subquery
questions.explanation: This describes the central operation taught in this lesson.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the sample queries is correct?
options: The query result depends on the input rows and the SQL condition
SQL always returns rows in insertion order
Aliases permanently rename source columns
A SELECT query always changes stored data
questions.answer: The query result depends on the input rows and the SQL condition
questions.explanation: SQL result sets are determined by the selected source rows and query expressions.

questions.prompt: Why should an SQL learner inspect expected output?
options: To verify the query's meaning against actual sample data
To make every query return the same rows
To avoid using a WHERE clause
To force a database-specific syntax
questions.answer: To verify the query's meaning against actual sample data
questions.explanation: Expected output helps detect misunderstandings about filtering, grouping, duplicates or comparisons.

options: Use explicit conditions and test edge cases
Omit conditions to shorten every query
Assume NULL behaves like zero
Rely on unspecified row order
questions.answer: Use explicit conditions and test edge cases
questions.explanation: Explicit query logic and edge-case testing make results easier to reason about.

questions.prompt: What should be done when a feature differs between database engines?
options: Label the dialect and verify the target engine's support
Assume all SQL engines behave identically
Remove the compatibility note
Silently replace the syntax without explanation
questions.answer: Label the dialect and verify the target engine's support
questions.explanation: Dialect-aware teaching avoids promising features that the learner's runtime cannot execute.
